subcategory: giant moisture-loving perennial for bog gardens and pond margins

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring directly into rich, consistently moist to wet soil; this far-eastern Russian giant needs several seasons to build the massive root crown that supports its towering flower plumes.

directions: Plant divisions in deep, humus-rich soil that never dries out, siting this plant at a pond margin, streambank, or low wet spot where its roots can stay constantly damp. Filipendula kamtschatica is the largest meadowsweet in cultivation, native to Kamchatka, Sakhalin, and northern Japan, sending up coarse, palmately lobed leaves to rival rhubarb and then towering, frothy plumes of white to pale-pink flowers in mid to late summer that can reach well over six feet. It is extremely cold hardy, surviving brutal far-eastern Russian winters, but performs poorly anywhere soil moisture is inconsistent. Give it room away from smaller perennials, since a mature clump eventually occupies several square feet and casts considerable shade of its own.

subcategory: compact Japanese woodland perennial for shaded borders

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in dappled shade; unlike its giant relatives this compact Japanese species is sized for ordinary borders and woodland edges.

directions: Set divisions into consistently moist, organically rich soil in a lightly shaded site, mulching to keep roots cool through summer. Native to the mountains of Honshu, Japan, Filipendula multijuga forms a neat clump of deeply cut, fern-like foliage topped from early to midsummer by dense, fuzzy plumes of rose-pink flowers held well above the leaves on wiry stems. It is far more manageably scaled than F. rubra or F. kamtschatica, making it a good choice for a shaded perennial border or the margin of a woodland stream where a smaller meadowsweet is wanted. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and flowering.

subcategory: diminutive alpine ephemeral for scree and trough gardens

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall into a gritty, sharply drained scree or trough mix and leave outdoors through winter; seed requires several months of cold to break dormancy and germinate the following spring.

directions: Steer's head is a true alpine ephemeral of the Sierra Nevada, Cascades, and Rocky Mountains, emerging through gravelly, barely-thawed scree within days of snowmelt to bloom while still nearly buried, then vanishing underground again by early summer once the soil dries. It needs extremely sharp drainage year-round and almost no supplemental water during its long summer dormancy, which makes it a specialist alpine-trough or scree-bed subject rather than a conventional border plant. The tiny pink-and-white flowers, shaped uncannily like a cow's skull, are easy to overlook but reward patience once a colony establishes. Mark its dormant position carefully, since the plant leaves no trace above ground for most of the year.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall ahead of winter rains into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; this chaparral native germinates most reliably with the heat and ash cues it receives naturally after wildfire.

directions: Golden eardrops is a California chaparral specialist famous for erupting in huge numbers on recently burned hillsides, where smoke and heat break the dormancy of long-buried seed banks, then fading out again over a few years as surrounding shrubs regrow and shade the site. In the garden it behaves as a short-lived, biennial-to-perennial wildflower, forming a basal rosette of blue-green, deeply cut foliage before sending up tall, branching, wand-like stems hung with clusters of bright golden-yellow, spurred flowers in late spring and summer. It wants lean, fast-draining soil and full sun, with no summer irrigation once established, mimicking the dry chaparral slopes it comes from. Allow seed to scatter and self-sow to keep a planting going, since individual plants are not long-lived.

subcategory: airy European foliage perennial for borders and cottage gardens

planting.note: Start seed indoors with a period of cold stratification, or set out nursery divisions after the last frost into average, well-drained soil; established plants need little further attention.

directions: Lesser meadow-rue is grown chiefly for its finely divided, blue-green, columbine-like foliage, which forms an airy, see-through haze through a border from spring onward. In mid to late summer wiry stems carry loose, open panicles of small, nodding, greenish-yellow flowers with conspicuous tufted stamens rather than showy petals, giving the plant a soft, textural presence rather than bold color. Native across much of Europe and widely naturalized, it tolerates average garden soil and part shade to full sun, and once established requires almost no maintenance beyond an occasional spring tidy-up. Use it as a filler among bolder-flowered perennials, where its lacy foliage sets off neighboring color without competing with it.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out small plants in spring into lean, sharply drained, alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage matters more than fertility for this alpine species.

directions: Shining scabious is a true alpine, native to rocky meadows and scree slopes of the European Alps, Apennines, and Balkans, forming a low basal rosette of glossy leaves (lucida means shining) that gives the species its name. From mid to late summer it sends up short, wiry stems carrying rose-lilac pincushion flower heads typical of the genus, scaled down to suit a rock garden rather than a border. It demands sharp drainage and lean, preferably alkaline soil, since rich or poorly drained ground quickly rots the crown. Grow it in a rock garden, raised bed, or trough alongside other true alpines rather than with lusher perennial border scabious like S. caucasica.
